issues.body:
Line ~170: `local readiness_ask="${4:-ASK {}}"`.

Bash terminates a `${var:-word}` expansion at the first unescaped `}`. It does NOT balance the `{` inside the default word. So this text parses as the expansion `${4:-ASK {` followed by a LITERAL `}` that is concatenated onto whatever the expansion produced.

Reproduced verbatim:
  FEATURE_READY_ASK='ASK { ?f <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#hasGeometry> ?g }'
  start_fuseki corpus.nt 3041 log.txt "$FEATURE_READY_ASK"
  -> QUERY SENT >>>ASK { ?f <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#hasGeometry> ?g }}<<<
(1 `{`, 2 `}` - a SPARQL parse error.)

Consequences, all on the new leg only:
1. Fuseki returns HTTP 400 for every readiness probe, the adapter exits non-zero, `ready=` never assigns, and the `while` loop runs to the FUSEKI_READY_S cap (default 300s) before `return 1`.
2. The elif branch fires every time: JENA_INDEX_READY_S="n/a", JENA_STATUS="partial: indexed-variant server not ready", and within10km_indexed is written as `ERROR\tserver-not-ready`. The feature is 100% inert - exactly the round-1 outcome, by a different mechanism.
3. Every geo-same-box run that reaches the jena leg now pays a silent ~5 minute stall after the base workloads, plus a JVM that loaded the 200k-triple feature corpus for nothing.

The no-argument path is unaffected by luck: `ASK {` + literal `}` == `ASK {}`, so the base server's probe is still correct. That is why this is invisible to a partial run and why it is worth pinning with a test.

This also demonstrates the leg has not been executed end-to-end since the round-1 fix, which is the direct cause of the remaining major below.
issues.fix_hint:
Never put a brace-containing default inside the expansion. Either:

  local default_ask='ASK {}'
  local readiness_ask="${4:-$default_ask}"

or branch explicitly:

  local readiness_ask='ASK {}'
  [ "$#" -ge 4 ] && readiness_ask="$4"

Then prove it: add a shell unit check (or a one-line self-test in the harness) that calls start_fuseki's argument handling with and without $4 and asserts the emitted query string is byte-equal to the input - a `printf '%s' "$readiness_ask" | grep -c '}'` style assertion goes red on the current code. Running `shellcheck` on this file would also be worth wiring, since it flags the mismatched-brace shape.
issues.title: start_fuseki's readiness default mis-parses: `${4:-ASK {}}` appends a literal `}` to the caller's query, so the feature readiness probe is invalid SPARQL and the indexed leg can never start

issues.body:
Round 1 asked for the observed count to be pinned in the header the way the verified sibling does. The units and limit concerns ARE addressed (uom:metre URI matching within10km.rq, explicit -1 limit), which is real progress. What is still missing is the evidence line.

within10km.rq records: "verified count-equal to sparq's expected.tsv (51) on the pinned 100k corpus", and documents at length (sq-a8anf) that an unverified Jena rendering silently produced all-zero counts that forced a retraction of the wave-1 nearest_k timings. This file carries only the runtime oracle statement.

Given the blocker above, nothing in this PR can have observed a count from this query. Two residual unknowns that only a real run settles:
- Whether Jena's spatial index, built over the feature->geometry corpus, indexes the FEATURE only (count 51) or both the feature and the geometry node (count 102 -> count-disagree -> permanently withheld).
- Whether `spatial:withinCircle` accepts a literal -1 limit argument, or rejects it at query-build time.

Both degrade to ERROR or count-disagree rather than to a false speed number, so the count oracle holds and this is major rather than blocker. But it means the workload may still never yield a usable row after the blocker is fixed.

Related, in geo-same-box.sh: FEATURE_READY_ASK only proves the triples are loaded. Fuseki may answer a plain BGP before its spatial index finishes building, in which case start_fuseki reports ready and the timed query runs against an empty index. The honest probe is the property function itself.
issues.fix_hint:
After fixing the blocker, run the leg against the pinned jar and record the observed count in the header in the sibling's form, e.g.: "verified count-equal to sparq's expected.tsv within10km (51) on the pinned 100k feature-modelled corpus, jena-fuseki-geosparql 5.4.0". If the observed count is 102, add a `?e geo:hasGeometry ?g .` guard and re-record.

Make the readiness probe exercise the index rather than the data:
  FEATURE_READY_ASK='PREFIX spatial: <http://jena.apache.org/spatial#> PREFIX uom: <http://www.opengis.net/def/uom/OGC/1.0/> ASK { ?e spatial:withinCircle (51 0 10000 uom:metre -1) }'
That returns false (count 0) until the spatial index is live, so a not-yet-indexed server can never be reported ready - and it would have surfaced the -1 / units questions during startup instead of as a timed-query ERROR.
issues.title: Still no recorded execution evidence - the query has never produced an observed count, and the readiness probe proves data-loaded, not index-built

issues.body:
Line ~343: `INDEX_PORT=$((FUSEKI_PORT + 2))`.

The header env-var table (lines 86-92) documents FUSEKI_PORT (3039) and GG_FUSEKI_PORT (default FUSEKI_PORT+1) as the ports this harness claims. FUSEKI_PORT+2 is now a third reserved port with no documentation and no override, so:
- a user who explicitly sets GG_FUSEKI_PORT=$((FUSEKI_PORT+2)) to dodge a busy 3040 collides with the indexed leg;
- on a box where 3041 is already occupied by an unrelated service, the second JVM fails to bind and the readiness probe talks to that foreign server. The dataset-identifying ASK mitigates this (good), but only if the foreign server lacks hasGeometry triples.

Same class of exposure the base leg already has, but newly widened without a documented knob.
issues.fix_hint:
Introduce `INDEX_FUSEKI_PORT="${INDEX_FUSEKI_PORT:-$((FUSEKI_PORT + 2))}"` next to GG_FUSEKI_PORT at line ~124 and add a line to the header env-var block:
  #   INDEX_FUSEKI_PORT  the indexed-radius leg's fuseki port (default FUSEKI_PORT+2)
issues.title: INDEX_PORT is hard-coded to FUSEKI_PORT+2, not overridable, and not listed in the header env-var block

issues.body:
Line ~233 runs `gen.sh 100000 feature` before the `want jena-geosparql` guard. On a sparq-only run (ONLY=sparq), or on a run where the Jena jar is absent and the leg gracefully skips, the harness still pays a full-corpus awk pass plus two `wc -l` passes and writes a second ~200k-line file into the cached /tmp/geo tree.

The gen.sh header explicitly notes CI may key actions/cache on /tmp/geo, so this roughly triples the cached geo footprint (points-100000.nt plus points-feature-100000.nt at ~2x the triples) for every consumer, including ones that never use the feature variant.
issues.fix_hint: Move the FEATURE_CORPUS / FEATURE_TRIPLES computation inside the `if want jena-geosparql` block (or guard it with `if want jena-geosparql; then ... fi`), and default FEATURE_TRIPLES/FEATURE_CORPUS to "n/a" for the envelope's scale string so the sparq-only envelope does not claim a variant that was never built.
issues.title: FEATURE_CORPUS is generated unconditionally, even for ONLY=sparq runs that never start Jena

issues.body:
Two soft spots in the new shutdown path:

1. `stop_fuseki` sends only SIGTERM (`kill "$FUSEKI_PID"`). Because the JVM was started inside a command-substitution subshell it is orphaned, so the following `wait` cannot reap it and returns immediately - the real wait is wait_fuseki_stopped's 30s poll. A JVM that is slow to honour SIGTERM (a large in-memory dataset teardown is not instant) trips the hard-coded 30s cap, and the run then records `ERROR/base-server-still-running` and skips the indexed leg entirely - even though INDEX_PORT was free the whole time and the leg could have run. Conservative and honest, but it converts a transient shutdown delay into a permanently missing workload.

2. `wait_fuseki_stopped` returns 0 on ANY non-zero exit from the adapter. A transient HTTP 500 or a parse hiccup from a still-alive server reads as 'stopped'. The consequence here is mild (the next server is on a different port anyway), but the function's contract says 'port is free' and it actually tests 'the query did not succeed'.
issues.fix_hint:
Escalate: after SIGTERM, poll briefly, then `kill -9` before giving up:
  kill "$FUSEKI_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
  wait_fuseki_stopped "$port" || { kill -9 "$FUSEKI_PID" 2>/dev/null || true; wait_fuseki_stopped "$port"; }
Make the 30s cap a variable (e.g. FUSEKI_STOP_S="${FUSEKI_STOP_S:-30}"). For (2), prefer a liveness test that cannot be confused with an error, e.g. `kill -0 "$pid"` on the recorded PID, falling back to the port probe only when the PID is unknown.
issues.title: stop_fuseki has no SIGKILL escalation and wait_fuseki_stopped treats any adapter failure as 'stopped'

issues.body:
The new `row.sparq_oracle_workload` correctly records that within10km_indexed's count oracle is borrowed from within10km - that closes the round-1 gap and is byte-stable for existing envelopes (cc.sparq_oracle_workload is undefined there, so no committed snapshot moves). Verified.

What the row still does not say is that this timing was measured on a DIFFERENT dataset: 2x the triples, feature->geometry modelled, on a separate server. Only the suite-level `scale` string mentions it. A reader scanning the rows sees `within10km` (Jena filter scan, slow) next to `within10km_indexed` (Jena indexed, fast) with `rows: 51` on both and no per-row signal that the substrate changed. Nothing false is asserted, but the corpus asymmetry is the single most load-bearing caveat for that row and it lives two levels away from it.
issues.fix_hint:
Carry a per-row corpus note alongside the oracle note. In geo-same-box.sh add e.g. `"corpus_variant": "feature-modelled (2x triples, separate server)"` to `cross["within10km_indexed"]`, and propagate it here next to sparq_oracle_workload:
  if (cc.corpus_variant) row.corpus_variant = cc.corpus_variant;
issues.title: The published row carries the borrowed-oracle provenance but not the fact that it ran on a different corpus

issues.body:
The guard asserts FEATURE_OUT.tmp has exactly 2 * lines(OUT). That catches gross truncation (a killed awk, a full disk), which is worth having.

It does not catch the shape drift the round-1 nit was about: if bench_geo ever emits two triples per entity, OUT has 2N lines and the transform emits 4N == 2 * 2N, so the guard passes while the corpus is silently corrupt (the second triple's subject would be rewritten to a /geometry> IRI and given a bogus hasGeometry edge). The transform's real preconditions - one triple per line, subject IS the entity, `<...>` subject form - remain unasserted. Since FEATURE_OUT is cached under /tmp/geo and reused, such corruption would persist across runs.

I re-verified the transform is correct against today's generator: the WKT literal's internal space splits across $3/$4 and rebuilding via `$1 = geometry` with OFS=" " restores the original single-space separators byte-for-byte, including the negative-longitude case.
issues.title: The 2x line-count post-condition does not catch the drift class it was added to guard

verdict.summary:
Round 2 genuinely fixes the round-1 blocker's structure: the PID now survives the command substitution via $TMP/fuseki.pid (verified), the indexed leg moved to a distinct port (FUSEKI_PORT+2, clear of GG_FUSEKI_PORT), stop is followed by a port-free poll, JENA_STATUS records 'partial: ...' instead of a blanket 'ok', the ERROR rows now loop over $INDEX_WORKLOADS, the scale string carries the feature-corpus triple count, gen.sh gained a post-condition, and the ingester propagates sparq_oracle_workload. I re-verified the awk transform byte-for-byte against generate_corpus (crates/sparq-geo/examples/bench_geo.rs:86-97) and confirmed the adapter's stdout contract makes the new `cut -f2 == 1` readiness check correct for the base ASK {} probe.

But the fix introduced a NEW blocker of equal effect. `local readiness_ask="${4:-ASK {}}"` does not parse the way it reads: bash closes the parameter expansion at the FIRST unescaped `}`, so the default word is `ASK {` and the trailing `}` is a literal appended to the EXPANDED value. Reproduced directly:
  start_fuseki corpus 3041 log "ASK { ?f <...hasGeometry> ?g }"
  -> QUERY SENT >>>ASK { ?f <...hasGeometry> ?g }}<<<
That is invalid SPARQL (1 open brace, 2 close). Fuseki answers 400, the adapter exits non-zero, the readiness loop never succeeds, start_fuseki spins the full FUSEKI_READY_S (default 300s) and returns 1. So within10km_indexed is permanently ERROR/server-not-ready and every geo-same-box run gains a 5-minute stall. The unset case works only by luck (`ASK {` + `}` == `ASK {}`), so the base leg is unaffected.

Net effect is unchanged from round 1 - the indexed leg still cannot run - which also means the new .rq has still never been executed. Its units/limit concerns are fixed (uom:metre URI, explicit -1), but it still records no observed count, unlike its sibling within10km.rq which pins "verified count-equal to sparq's expected.tsv (51)". The count oracle does contain the damage: no false timing can ship.
